t: On May 4, 1919, over 4,000 students marched to Tiananmen against the Treaty of Versailles’ award of Germany’s rights in Shandong to Japan and against the Beijing government’s weak response.

When the government arrested nearly 1,000 students in June, workers and merchants struck in their support, the movement’s centre moved to Shanghai, and the government dismissed three officials accused of collaborating with Japan.

A turning point of the New Culture Movement, which called for “Mr. Science” and “Mr. Democracy” in place of “Mr. Confucius”, it made written vernacular Chinese the language of modern literature and helped give rise to the Chinese Communist Party.
dyk: In 1917 Chen Hengzhe published the short story One Day in an overseas student quarterly, a year before Lu Xun’s Diary of a Madman, which has often been wrongly credited as the first vernacular Chinese fiction.
ev: Japan’s Twenty-One Demands become known to the Chinese public and provoke anti-Japanese feeling
China enters World War I on the side of the Triple Entente, and Hu Shih argues for the vernacular in “Preliminary discussion on literary reform”
The leak of the secret Sino-Japanese Joint Defence Agreement signed by Premier Duan Qirui sparks a student protest movement
On May 4 over 4,000 students gather in front of Tiananmen to protest the Shandong terms of the Treaty of Versailles
After the June 3 arrests a general strike in Shanghai forces the dismissal of Cao Rulin, Zhang Zongxiang and Lu Zongyu, and China’s delegates refuse to sign the treaty
Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao are among the founders of the Chinese Communist Party
Mao Zedong calls the May Fourth Movement a new stage in China’s bourgeois-democratic revolution

f.where: Beijing, where it began at Tiananmen and in the universities; Shanghai, where the strikes of June 1919 moved its centre; the larger cities across China, Guangzhou among them; Chinese students in Paris; echoes in Penang and Singapore in British Malaya.
f.period: The New Culture Movement, 1915–1921, its broader setting; the demonstration of May 4, 1919 and the student strikes of May; the June 3 arrests and the Shanghai general strike, ended on June 12, 1919; China’s refusal to sign the Treaty of Versailles; the founding of the Chinese Communist Party in 1921.
f.figures: Cai Yuanpei, principal of Peking University, who resigned in protest; Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao, leaders of the movement and founders of the Chinese Communist Party; Hu Shih, advocate of the vernacular; Chen Hengzhe and Lu Xun, writers of early vernacular fiction; Zhou Enlai and Chen Tanqiu; Kuomintang members such as Luo Jialun.
f.outcome: The dismissal of Cao Rulin, Zhang Zongxiang and Lu Zongyu and China’s refusal to sign the Treaty of Versailles, a largely symbolic victory, since Japan kept Shandong for the moment; the rise of written vernacular Chinese and modern Chinese literature, and of Marxism and the Chinese Communist Party.
